\chapter{Four Things You Wear}
\label{ch:ur-clothing}
\hlchaptermodality{14}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a shirt, shoe, cap and coat in Urdu, and sort each word by which direction it was borrowed: into Urdu, out of Urdu into English, or straight from English.}

Name \ur{قمیض}, \ur{جوتا}, \ur{ٹوپی} and \ur{کوٹ}, then sort all four by the direction their loan travelled: Persian and Arabic into Urdu, Urdu out into English, or English straight into Urdu — three directions in one small set of words.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[qamīz]{\ur{قمیض} — \textquotedblleft{}shirt,\textquotedblright{} and a word that meets its English cousin in a wardrobe}

\label{lesson:UR-C14-qamiz}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{\ur{نیلا}}'s long trip forward into English \textbf{aniline}. This lesson opens a new chapter — four things you wear — and its first word makes an even stranger connection than blue did.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{قمیض}} — \emph{qamīz} — \textbf{shirt}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میری} \ur{قمیض} \ur{نیلی} \ur{ہے۔}} — \emph{merī qamīz nīlī hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}My shirt is blue.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{قمیض}} is feminine — that is why \textbf{\ur{نیلا}} becomes \textbf{\ur{نیلی}} here.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
From the right edge: \textbf{\ur{ق}}, \textbf{\ur{م}}, \textbf{\ur{ی}}, \textbf{\ur{ض}}.

\textbf{\ur{ق}} \emph{qāf} is a new letter, said with the back of the tongue drawn further back in the throat than \textbf{\ur{ک}} \emph{kāf} — in relaxed speech many speakers merge the two, but careful and formal pronunciation keeps them apart. \textbf{\ur{ض}} \emph{zād} is also new: like \textbf{\ur{ظ}}, already known from \textbf{\ur{حافظ}}, it represents the plain \textbf{z} sound in Urdu, even though Arabic once told the two letters apart. Urdu keeps both spellings without keeping the sound distinction Arabic makes.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{قمیض}} is borrowed from Classical Persian \emph{qamīs}, from Arabic \textbf{qamīṣ}, probably from Latin \textbf{camisia}, from Proto-West Germanic \textbf{*hamiþi}, from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*\'{k}am-}, \textquotedblleft{}cover, clothes.\textquotedblright{} That same Latin \textbf{camisia} also gives French \textbf{chemise}, borrowed straight into English as \textbf{chemise}. Two roads out of one Late Latin word: one east through Arabic and Persian into Urdu, one north through French into English — and both landed, centuries later, meaning a piece of clothing worn on the upper body.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{qamīz} — shirt; then \textbf{merī qamīz nīlī hai}
  \item \emph{Name:} \textbf{\ur{ق}} and \textbf{\ur{ض}}, the two new letters, and what each is close to — \textbf{\ur{ک}} and \textbf{\ur{ظ}}
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{qamīz} $\leftarrow$ Latin \textbf{camisia} $\to$ English \textbf{chemise}, two roads, one Late Latin source
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ur{نیلی} \ur{قمیض}} — a blue shirt
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} mean, and is it masculine or feminine? (\textbf{Shirt}; \textbf{feminine}.) Which English word probably shares \textbf{\ur{قمیض}}'s Latin source? (\textbf{Chemise.}) What does \textbf{\ur{آپ} \ur{کا} \ur{نام} \ur{کیا} \ur{ہے؟}} ask, and which word is fixed there regardless of who is asked? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}What is your name?\textquotedblright{}}; \textbf{\ur{کا}}, in this frame.) Name the two new letters in this word and one letter each is close to. (\textbf{\ur{ق}, close to \ur{ک}; \ur{ض}, close to \ur{ظ}.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%82\%D9\%85\%DB\%8C\%D8\%B6}{Wiktionary: \ur{قمیض}}, \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/chemise}{Wiktionary: chemise}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jūtā]{\ur{جوتا} — \textquotedblleft{}shoe,\textquotedblright{} a cousin of yoke, and a cousin of yoga too}

\label{lesson:UR-C14-juta}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} and its long-shot cousin English \textbf{chemise}. This word's English cousin is even closer, and its Sanskrit cousin is a word you likely already know.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{جوتا}} — \emph{jūtā} — \textbf{shoe}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{جوتا} \ur{کالا} \ur{ہے۔}} — \emph{merā jūtā kālā hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}My shoe is black.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{جوتا}} is masculine — that is why \textbf{\ur{کالا}} stays \textbf{\ur{کالا}} here rather than becoming \textbf{\ur{کالی}}.

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
From the right edge: \textbf{\ur{ج}}, \textbf{\ur{و}}, \textbf{\ur{ت}}, \textbf{\ur{ا}}.

\textbf{\ur{ت}} \emph{te} is new, and it shares its base shape with \textbf{\ur{ٹ}}, already known from \textbf{\ur{ٹھیک}}: the same scoop, but \textbf{\ur{ت}} carries two dots above where \textbf{\ur{ٹ}} carries a small raised loop instead. Two dots make it plain dental \emph{t}; the loop makes it the retroflex \emph{ṭ} the tongue curls back for.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{jūtā} continues Sauraseni Prakrit \emph{jutta}, \textquotedblleft{}joined,\textquotedblright{} from Sanskrit \emph{yukta}, \textquotedblleft{}joined, yoked,\textquotedblright{} from Proto-Indo-European \textbf{*yewg-}, \textquotedblleft{}to yoke.\textquotedblright{} That root gives English \textbf{yoke} directly, the wooden bar that joins two oxen. It also gives Sanskrit its own word \textbf{yoga} — literally \textquotedblleft{}a joining, a yoking\textquotedblright{} — the same root, kept inside one language this time rather than split across two. \textbf{\ur{جوتا}} keeps the oldest, plainest sense: a thing joined onto the foot.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{jūtā} — shoe; then \textbf{merā jūtā kālā hai}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\ur{ت}}, two dots, plain \emph{t}; \textbf{\ur{ٹ}}, raised loop, retroflex \emph{ṭ}
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{jūtā} $\leftarrow$ \emph{yukta} $\leftarrow$ PIE \emph{*yewg-} $\to$ English \textbf{yoke}, and $\to$ Sanskrit's own \textbf{yoga}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ur{نیلی} \ur{قمیض}} and \textbf{\ur{کالا} \ur{جوتا}} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ur{جوتا}} mean, and is it masculine or feminine? (\textbf{Shoe}; \textbf{masculine}.) Name \textbf{\ur{جوتا}}'s two English-family cousins. (\textbf{Yoke, and Sanskrit's own yoga.}) What marks \textbf{\ur{ت}} apart from the already-known \textbf{\ur{ٹ}}? (\textbf{Two dots above, instead of a raised loop.}) When asking how someone is, does \textbf{kaise}/\textbf{kaisī} agree with your own gender or the gender of the person you're asking? (\textbf{The person you're asking.}) Recall \textbf{\ur{ٹھیک}}'s Hindi bridge — does it come before or after you can already read the Urdu form yourself? (\textbf{After.}) What line closes the take-leave dialogue this book opened early on? (\textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}, spoken by both voices.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AC\%D9\%88\%D8\%AA\%D8\%A7}{Wiktionary: \ur{جوتا}}, \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AF\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%A4}{Wiktionary: yukta}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ṭopī]{\ur{ٹوپی} — \textquotedblleft{}cap,\textquotedblright{} a dead end behind it, a loan ahead of it}

\label{lesson:UR-C14-topi}



\begin{quote}
Recall \textbf{\ur{جوتا}}, cousin of English \textbf{yoke} and Sanskrit \textbf{yoga}. This word has no such cousin behind it — but it made one of its own, going the other direction.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}} — \emph{ṭopī} — \textbf{cap, hat}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میری} \ur{ٹوپی} \ur{سفید} \ur{ہے۔}} — \emph{merī ṭopī safed hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}My cap is white.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}} is feminine, like \textbf{\ur{روٹی}} and \textbf{\ur{قمیض}}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}} is inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit \emph{ṭopiā}, \textquotedblleft{}helmet,\textquotedblright{} related to Sanskrit \emph{ṭopikā}. No further root is documented behind that — another honest dead end, like \textbf{\ur{روٹی}} and \textbf{\ur{کان}}.

But \textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}} did something those two never did: it left Urdu and Hindi and became an English word. \textbf{Topee}, first recorded in English between 1825 and 1835, is borrowed directly from Hindi \emph{ṭopī}, \textquotedblleft{}hat\textquotedblright{} — the lightweight sun hat worn across British India. \textbf{\ur{نیلا}}'s cousin \emph{nīlī} took four languages and a chemistry lab to become English \emph{aniline}. \textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}} simply walked straight into English as itself.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{ṭopī} — cap; then \textbf{merī ṭopī safed hai}
  \item \emph{Name:} \textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}}'s own root stops at Prakrit — a dead end, like \textbf{\ur{روٹی}}
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{ṭopī} $\to$ English \textbf{topee}, borrowed directly, no intermediate language
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{\ur{کالا} \ur{جوتا}} and \textbf{\ur{سفید} \ur{ٹوپی}} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}} mean, and is it masculine or feminine? (\textbf{Cap/hat}; \textbf{feminine}.) Does \textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}} have a documented root before Prakrit? (\textbf{No — a dead end.}) What English word borrows \textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}} directly, and roughly when? (\textbf{Topee, 1825–35.}) Recall the frame that put \textbf{\ur{ٹھیک}} inside a full sentence — say it now with \textbf{\ur{میں}}. (\textbf{\ur{میں} \ur{ٹھیک} \ur{ہوں۔}}) Does \textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}} need a conjugated verb to work as a farewell? (\textbf{No — it's used as a fixed formula, no agreement ending required.})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D9\%B9\%D9\%88\%D9\%BE\%DB\%8C}{Wiktionary: \ur{ٹوپی}}, \href{https://www.dictionary.com/browse/topee}{Dictionary.com: topee}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[koṭ]{\ur{کوٹ} — \textquotedblleft{}coat,\textquotedblright{} and every direction a loan can travel}

\label{lesson:UR-C14-koat}



\begin{quote}
Recall this chapter's three words: \textbf{\ur{قمیض}}, borrowed from Arabic through Persian; \textbf{\ur{جوتا}}, inherited all the way from Proto-Indo- European; \textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}}, borrowed \emph{out} of Urdu into English as \emph{topee}. This chapter's last word takes the shortest road of all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one word}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کوٹ}} — \emph{koṭ} — \textbf{coat}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{میرا} \ur{کوٹ} \ur{نیلا} \ur{ہے۔}} — \emph{merā koṭ nīlā hai.} — \textquotedblleft{}My coat is blue.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\ur{کوٹ}} is masculine.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{کوٹ}} is borrowed directly from English \textbf{coat} — a modern loan, one generation old rather than a thousand years. It happens to look identical to an older, unrelated \textbf{\ur{کوٹ}} meaning \textquotedblleft{}fort,\textquotedblright{} inherited from Sanskrit \emph{koṭṭa} — the two are homographs, not cousins, and the spelling gives no warning either way.

This book has named two layers before now: the inherited Indo-Aryan core, and the Persian-Arabic literary layer borrowed centuries ago. \textbf{\ur{کوٹ}} is the first clear example of a \textbf{third} layer — everyday English loans, arriving through more recent contact. And this chapter has now shown every direction a loanword can travel in one small set of four: Persian and Arabic \emph{into} Urdu (\textbf{\ur{قمیض}}), Urdu straight \emph{out} into English (\textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}}), and English straight \emph{into} Urdu (\textbf{\ur{کوٹ}}).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{koṭ} — coat; then \textbf{merā koṭ nīlā hai}
  \item \emph{Name:} three layers now — inherited, Persian-Arabic, and modern English
  \item \emph{Sort:} \textbf{\ur{قمیض}} in, \textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}} out, \textbf{\ur{کوٹ}} in — three loans, three directions
  \item \emph{Say it:} all four clothing words — \textbf{\ur{قمیض}, \ur{جوتا}, \ur{ٹوپی}, \ur{کوٹ}} — each with a color from the earlier chapter
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ur{کوٹ}} mean, and where does it come from? (\textbf{Coat}; \textbf{borrowed directly from English}.) Which of this chapter's four words was borrowed \emph{out of} Urdu rather than into it? (\textbf{\ur{ٹوپی}, into English as topee.}) Recall the farewell that closes almost any Urdu conversation — say it now. (\textbf{\ur{خدا} \ur{حافظ}.}) What does the standard reply to the wellbeing question say about the speaker? (\textbf{\ur{میں} \ur{ٹھیک} \ur{ہوں،} \ur{شکریہ} — \textquotedblleft{}I am fine, thank you.\textquotedblright{}})

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DA\%A9\%D9\%88\%D9\%B9}{Wiktionary: \ur{کوٹ}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
